quiz.question: What does the Linux Load Average metric primarily represent?
options: The instantaneous percentage of CPU utilization across all cores
The average number of tasks that are runnable (R) or in uninterruptible sleep (D) over time
The percentage of free physical RAM remaining in the system
The rate of disk write throughput in megabytes per second
quiz.explanation: Linux load average is not a CPU percentage. It measures the average demand for compute resources, counting tasks currently executing, waiting on CPU runqueues (R), and blocked on uninterruptible kernel I/O (D).

quiz.question: Which virtual filesystem interface exposes per-process memory mappings, open file descriptors, and runtime status?
options: /dev
/sys only
/proc/<PID>
/boot
quiz.explanation: /proc is a virtual pseudo-filesystem created dynamically by the kernel. Subdirectories named after process IDs (/proc/<PID>) expose status, fd, maps, and I/O counters for that specific process.

quiz.question: Which tool is best suited for sampling CPU instruction hot spots and call stacks with minimal performance overhead?
options: perf
journalctl only
free
ls
quiz.explanation: Linux perf uses hardware performance monitoring counters (PMUs) and kernel tracepoints to sample instruction execution and call stacks with low overhead, generating statistical flame graphs and symbol profiles.

quiz.question: What does sustained swap-in/out activity (si/so in vmstat) combined with high Memory PSI stalls indicate?
options: The physical CPU hardware has a broken core
Severe memory pressure and active page thrashing
The filesystem is always physically corrupted
A multi-threaded deadlock is definitively proven
quiz.explanation: When active anonymous application memory exceeds physical RAM, the kernel is forced to swap pages out to disk and read them back in on demand (si/so). Combined with high PSI memory stalls, this proves active memory thrashing.

quiz.question: What does strace primarily observe during an application's execution?
options: Every single CPU assembly instruction executed in user space
System calls crossing the user/kernel boundary and received signals
Only motherboard and disk drive temperature sensors
Only kernel boot timestamps
quiz.explanation: strace intercepts and records system calls made by a process and signals received, capturing system call names, arguments, return codes, and elapsed execution duration.

quiz.question: Why should an engineer correlate multiple diagnostic tools before concluding that storage I/O is the bottleneck?
options: Because all Linux performance tools always output identical data
Because high device utilization (%util) alone does not prove an application bottleneck without measuring request latency and blocked tasks
Because correlating tools completely removes all measurement overhead
Because modern SSDs cannot experience hardware degradation
quiz.explanation: A single metric can be misleading. High disk %util on modern NVMe drives may simply indicate parallel queue saturation without latency spikes. Engineers correlate iostat (await), vmstat (b, wa), and strace (-T) to confirm that the application is actually waiting on I/O.

In Linux, both processes and threads are represented internally by identical kernel task structures (task_struct). The clone() syscall controls the degree of sharing between parent and child:

A thread showing 100% CPU utilization may be doing productive work, or it may be spinning in an infinite loop, thrashing on lock contention, or repeatedly retrying failed syscalls. Never assume high CPU equals high productivity.

theorySections.title: 2. Kernel Interfaces: /proc, /sys, and /dev
paragraphs: Virtual filesystems · Process inspection · Device hierarchies · Load Average truth
Linux implements the Unix philosophy "everything is a file" by exposing kernel runtime state through three distinct virtual filesystems:
Dynamic window into kernel memory, process table, open file descriptors, memory mappings, and CPU stats.
Structured device hierarchy, block device queues, cgroups v2, and tunable kernel configuration parameters.
Character and block device nodes (e.g. /dev/null, /dev/nvme0n1) routing I/O directly to drivers.
Inspect live mock outputs from `/proc/status`, `/proc/meminfo`, `/proc/pressure/memory`, and `/sys`.

theorySections.title: 3. systemd, journald, and Kernel Ring Buffer Diagnostics
paragraphs: systemctl status · journalctl filtering · systemd-analyze critical-chain · dmesg OOM triage
When services fail or slow down, Linux engineers correlate user-space systemd service logs with kernel ring buffer messages:
Catches Out-of-Memory (OOM) killer terminations, NVMe timeout resets, PCIe link errors, and filesystem write failures.
Filters log events strictly for a specific service unit since the current system boot, preserving stdout/stderr output.

Diagnosing complex systems requires selecting the right instrument for each tier:
Focus on await (average completion latency in ms) and aqu-sz (queue depth). High %util alone does not prove an NVMe is bottlenecked if await remains sub-millisecond!

theorySections.title: 6. System-Call Profiling and Bottleneck Diagnosis
paragraphs: strace -c vs -T · Measurement perturbation · Profiling waiting vs computation
strace captures every syscall made by a process. Use -c for summary profiling and -T to measure syscall duration:

{`$ strace -f -c ./app % time seconds usecs/call calls errors syscall ------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ---------------- 84.12 4.120400 41204 100 fsync 12.40 0.608100 60 10000 write 2.10 0.102800 10 10000 read ------ ----------- ----------- --------- --------- ---------------- 100.00 4.831300 20100 total`} The Observer Effect (Perturbation Warning) strace stops execution on every syscall entry and exit. On system-call-heavy applications, attaching strace can slow execution by 2x to 10x! Always record baseline latency without strace first.
